history.heading: Polotsk and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania
paragraphs: East Slavic tribes settled the territory of present-day Belarus in the second half of the first millennium CE. The Principality of Polotsk, first mentioned in 862, was one of the earliest states in the region and part of the wider world of Kievan Rus'.

From the 13th and 14th centuries the Belarusian lands became part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, in which the Ruthenian language, an ancestor of Belarusian, was an official language. Francysk Skaryna printed one of the first books in an East Slavic language in 1517. The Grand Duchy united with Poland in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1569.

history.heading: Russian Empire and Soviet Belarus
paragraphs: The partitions of Poland in the late 18th century brought the region into the Russian Empire, which pursued Russification. A Belarusian People's Republic was proclaimed in 1918 but was short-lived, and the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic was established in 1919.

The Second World War was catastrophic: around a quarter of the population died, hundreds of villages were burned with their inhabitants, such as Khatyn, and the large Jewish community was almost entirely murdered in the Holocaust. In 1986 the Chernobyl disaster in neighbouring Ukraine contaminated large areas of southern Belarus.

history.heading: Independence and Lukashenko
paragraphs: Belarus became independent in 1991. Alexander Lukashenko was elected president in 1994 and has ruled ever since, building an authoritarian system and keeping much of the Soviet-style economy.

The 2020 presidential election, widely considered fraudulent, sparked the largest protests in the country's history. They were violently suppressed, and opposition leaders, including Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, went into exile. In 2022 Belarus allowed Russia to use its territory to invade Ukraine.

culture.heading: Language and identity
paragraphs: Belarusian and Russian are both official languages, but Russian is dominant in daily life, education and media, while Belarusian is closely tied to national identity. Most believers are Orthodox Christians, with a significant Catholic minority.
The white-red-white flag, used by the democratic opposition, and the official red-green flag represent competing visions of national identity.

culture.heading: Heritage and food
paragraphs: Mir Castle and Nesvizh Castle are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, as is Białowieża Forest, shared with Poland, home to the European bison. Painter Marc Chagall was born in Vitebsk, and Nobel laureate Svetlana Alexievich is Belarusian.
Potatoes are central to Belarusian cuisine, especially draniki (potato pancakes), along with machanka, kalduny and rye bread. Ice hockey is the most popular sport.

politics.heading: Authoritarian state
paragraphs: Belarus is formally a presidential republic, but power is concentrated in the president, who has ruled since 1994. Elections are not recognised as free or fair by Western observers, independent media and opposition parties have been suppressed, and there are many political prisoners.
A 2022 constitutional referendum expanded the role of the All-Belarusian People's Assembly and, in 2023, Russia stationed tactical nuclear weapons in Belarus.

politics.heading: Alliance with Russia
paragraphs: Belarus and Russia form a "Union State" with close economic, political and military integration. Belarus is a member of the Eurasian Economic Union and the CSTO. The European Union, the United States and others have imposed sanctions over the 2020 crackdown and the war in Ukraine.

economy.heading: State-dominated economy
paragraphs: Belarus retains a large state sector. Industry includes tractors and heavy trucks (such as BelAZ), machinery, petrochemicals, potash fertilisers and food products. Agriculture, especially dairy and potatoes, is also important. The country has a relatively developed IT sector, though many specialists left after 2020.

The economy depends heavily on Russia, which supplies cheap energy and is the main export market. Western sanctions have redirected trade toward Russia and China. The currency is the Belarusian ruble.
